newsitem.title: USA: New Chicago Archbishop George pleads for unity.
newsitem.headline: New Chicago Archbishop George pleads for unity.

text.p: Archbishop Francis George was installed Wednesday as leader of the nation's third-largest Roman Catholic archdiocese, delivering a strongly worded homily calling for racial harmony to his Chicago flock.

"In the church, every racial and cultural difference must be made public, so that everyone can come to know how Christ can be black, or white, or brown or yellow or red," George said during the elaborate ceremony at Chicago's Holy Name Cathedral.

"If I do not know any Mexicans, or Russians, or Africans, or Chicagoans, then I cannot experience personally how Christ can be Mexican, and Russian, and African and Chicagoan," George said in his first formal address to Chicago's 2.3 million member Catholics.
"The differences must always be made public but always in a way that they can be shared so that they can enrich everyone," he said.
A representative of Pope John Paul II helped George don his mitre and handed him his crosier, a curved wooden staff symbolic of the responsibility of shepherding his flock.

George acknowledged he was a surprise appointment by the Pope to succeed the late Cardinal Joseph Bernardin, who died of cancer in November, to head the nation's third-largest archdiocese after New York and Los Angeles.

He was formerly archbishop in Portland, Ore., for 10 months and prior to that served in Yakima, Wash., and spent a dozen years in Rome at the headquarters of his religious order, the Missionary Oblates of Mary Immaculate.

A highly intellectual cleric, George, 60, holds doctoral degrees in philosophy and theology and was seen as somewhat conservative compared to the moderate Bernardin, but not doctrinaire. He walks with a limp, a result of a childhood bout with polio.
As befitting an archdiocese with a growing Hispanic, Filipino and black membership, he urged local church leaders to harmonise society's racial and cultural differences.
"In our national experience, unity has been forged from diversity in less than successful ways. Unity has been sometimes been bought at the expense of differences," he said.

"The church must work as well to see that those people often overlooked in church and society especially the poor, the most vulnerable, the unborn and the dying, must be made visible both in the church and in society. The church must work to create a neighbourhood in which everyone can be at home," he said.
In contrast to his predecessor's 1982 introductory homily, George said he was not intimate enough with his 1,000 diocesan priests to ask them to call him "brother," as Bernardin did.
"Chicago was and is a city of neighbourhoods," said George, who was born, raised and ordained in the city. "For starters, if it's alright with you, I will say only that I am Francis, your neighbour."
"I never imagined I would be here today, taking on this mission ... If surprise is a sign of God's presence then God is with us in force today," he said.

Flashing a lively sense of humour, George recalled a Portland parishioner asking him if the loss of the city's archbishop might result in a trade where Chicago basketball star Michael Jordan might be coaxed to Portland.
"Now that would be a surprise," George said to laughter.
